content: Drug-induced skin reactions can manifest in a spectrum of clinical presentations, ranging from mild maculopapular rashes to life-threatening conditions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) or toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), which may result in mortality. Even milder reactions can significantly impact patient adherence to prescribed medications. The underlying mechanisms of these reactions remain incompletely understood. However, there is emerging evidence suggesting that genetic testing prior to treatment initiation may help predict and prevent such adverse reactions in certain cases. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of prospective pharmacogenetic screening in reducing the incidence of drug-induced skin reactions in a patient population. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Skin Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and LILACS, up to July 2018. Additionally, five trial registries were reviewed, and reference lists of relevant studies and reviews were examined to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) for inclusion. The inclusion criteria for the review were RCTs involving participants who underwent prospective pharmacogenetic screening to identify genetic variants associated with hypersensitivity reactions. These participants were compared to those who did not undergo such screening. The study population included individuals of any age, gender, or ethnicity who were prescribed drugs known to cause delayed-type hypersensitivity reactions. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were employed for data collection and analysis. Two independent reviewers screened all identified titles and abstracts for eligibility. Due to the inclusion of only one study, many planned data analyses could not be performed. The quality of the included study was assessed using the GRADE framework. The primary outcomes of interest were the incidence of severe skin rashes with systemic symptoms (e.g., fever, multi-organ involvement) and long-term sequelae (e.g., scarring of eyelids or lung tissue). Secondary outcomes included hospitalization due to drug-induced skin reactions, blistering skin reactions (e.g., SJS, hypersensitivity syndrome), and mortality. The single included study was a randomized, double-blind, controlled, multicenter trial involving 1956 adult participants (74% male, mean age 42 years) across 265 centers in 19 countries. All participants were HIV-1 positive and had not previously received abacavir. Participants requiring an antiretroviral regimen containing abacavir were randomized to either a prospective screening group, which underwent human leukocyte antigen (HLA) Class I, locus B, allele 57:01 (HLA-B57:01) testing prior to treatment, or a control group, which received standard care without prospective HLA-B57:01 screening. Those testing positive for HLA-B57:01 were not prescribed abacavir but were instead given alternative antiretroviral therapy. Retrospective HLA-B57:01 testing was performed in the control group. The trial lasted six months, with participants monitored for six weeks. Assessments were conducted at study entry, baseline (day one of abacavir treatment), and at weeks one, two, and six. The study was funded by GlaxoSmithKline, the manufacturer of abacavir. The trial did not evaluate the primary outcomes of the review, nor did it measure secondary outcomes in isolation. However, it assessed hypersensitivity reactions, which included but were not limited to the secondary outcomes of hypersensitivity syndrome (HSS) and SJS/TEN. The results indicated that prospective HLA-B57:01 screening likely reduces the incidence of hypersensitivity reactions to abacavir. The risk of clinically diagnosed HSS was lower in the screening group (risk ratio [RR] 0.43, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.28 to 0.67; 1650 participants; moderate-quality evidence). Similarly, the risk of immunologically confirmed HSS was reduced (RR 0.02, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.37; 1644 participants; moderate-quality evidence). Immunological confirmation was based on a positive epicutaneous patch test conducted six to ten weeks after clinical diagnosis. The study demonstrated a low risk of bias in five out of seven domains. However, there was a high risk of detection bias, as hypersensitivity reactions were diagnosed by the principal investigator at each recruitment site without predefined clinical criteria. Additionally, there was a high risk of attrition bias due to the exclusion of participants with incomplete follow-up data. Sensitivity analyses based on the intention-to-treat population were performed, yielding results consistent with the primary analysis. The overall quality of the study was rated as moderate using GRADE criteria. In conclusion, prospective HLA-B57:01 screening likely reduces the risk of severe hypersensitivity skin reactions to abacavir in HIV-1 positive patients. However, these findings are based on a single study with notable risks of detection and attrition bias. The trial did not assess the primary outcomes of severe skin rashes with systemic symptoms or long-term effects, and only one secondary outcome (hypersensitivity reaction) was evaluated. No evidence was found regarding hospitalization, mortality, or long-term complications resulting from drug-induced skin injuries. Furthermore, no eligible studies were identified for genetic testing related to severe drug-induced skin reactions involving other drugs or drug classes. Additional clinical trials focusing on other drugs and diverse patient populations are needed to inform policy changes aimed at preventing adverse skin reactions associated with drug treatments.
